Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
• 26-year-old man with known asthma presents with 3-hour history of chest tightness, mild dyspnea, wheeze and non-productive cough after a recent viral URI and 1-week lapse in inhaler use — consistent with an acute asthma exacerbation.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Sudden chest tightness started ~3 h ago; feels unable to take full breath.  
• Associated symptoms: Mild exertional shortness of breath (none at rest), wheeze, dry cough. Recent “cold” last week with sore throat & runny nose now improving.  
• Pertinent negatives: No chest pain, no productive sputum, no hemoptysis; denies drug allergies.  
• Past medical history: Physician-diagnosed asthma (severe exacerbation with intubation age 16–17); allergic rhinitis/hay-fever; childhood eczema; childhood milk-protein allergy.  
• Medications: Salbutamol (Ventolin) SABA inhaler and beclomethasone (Clenil Modulite) ICS inhaler — both ran out 1 week ago; no current supply.  
• Allergies: Environmental (dust); no medication allergies.  
• Family history: Father asthma; mother eczema.  
• Social / preventive: University student, age 26; smoking/alcohol status not discussed.

Examination:
• Tele-consult only; no vitals obtained.  
• Patient speaking full sentences, not breathless at rest.  
• Reports mild dyspnea on stair climbing; no acute distress observed via video.  
• No other physical findings available.

Impression:
• Most likely: Acute asthma exacerbation precipitated by viral upper-respiratory infection and interruption of controller therapy.  
   – Supported by history of asthma, recent URI, cessation of ICS/SABA, current wheeze, chest tightness, exertional SOB.  
• Alternative considerations (less likely):  
   – Viral acute bronchitis with reactive airways (overlaps with above).  
   – Community-acquired pneumonia or pulmonary embolism unlikely given absence of fever, sputum, pleuritic pain, risk factors.

Plan:
• Prescriptions sent electronically:  
   – Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler PRN.  
   – Beclomethasone (Clenil Modulite) inhaler; resume regular daily use once acute episode settles.  
   – Oral corticosteroid burst (e.g., prednisolone) 2 tablets each morning for 5 days; counselled on potential mood change, hyperglycemia, rash, nausea, headache.  
• Spacer device prescription and usage instructions provided.  
• Education: Use Ventolin as needed; if requiring doses more frequently than every 3 hours or if symptoms worsen (increasing SOB, chest tightness, light-headedness) seek urgent medical attention.  
• Rest advised; may self-certify first 7 days off work.  
• Follow-up: Contact primary care or return to service if no improvement after steroid course or earlier if deterioration.

Quality checks:

● Missing/expected elements:
  – No vital signs, oxygen saturation, peak-flow measurement obtained.
  – Smoking status, vaccination status (influenza, pneumococcal) not discussed.
  – Exact steroid name/dose not documented.

● Transcript vs DDx conflicts:
  – None noted; DDx aligns with transcript.

● Transcript quality:
  – Clear history but unavoidable minor audio dropouts; lacks objective exam and vitals typical of tele-consult.
